Biblia Pauperum, the Bible of the Poor, was a picture book pairing scenes from Christ's life with Old Testament foreshadowings, described in this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. A series of forty or fifty pages, each divided into nine sections, puts the Gospel scene at the centre, prophets above and below, and Old Testament scenes at the sides.

Corner texts explain the links, making the book a picture concordance of the two Testaments, gathering the Church's traditional reading of types and figures as taught in liturgy and preaching. Though called the poor man's Bible, it likely served preachers and the literate too. The entry presents a medieval teaching aid in pictures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bullarium:
A Bullarium gathers bulls and similar papal documents, whether general or tied to one order, house, or place. The name came from the canonist Laertius Cherubini, whose 1586 folio of 1,404 pages held 922 papal constitutions from Gregory VII to the reigning Sixtus V. Later collections followed his model, but three cautions govern them all.

First, each editor chose by his own judgment, so no collection held official standing. The exception is Benedict XIV's first volume of his own bulls, sent to Bologna in 1746 as a source of law. Second, no collection claimed completeness, or even all constitutions of general interest. Third, editors meant at first to exclude pronouncements already inside canon law's corpus, aiming instead to rescue enactments the corpus compilers had missed or popes had issued since. Mazzutellus's 1579 volume of 723 documents shows the form before Cherubini fixed it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caeremoniale-:
The Caeremoniale Episcoporum is the book of rites and ceremonies for bishops and lesser prelates at Mass, Vespers, and other functions in metropolitan, cathedral, and collegiate churches. It also settles precedence among clergy and official layfolk. After Sixtus V set up the Congregation of Sacred Rites in 1587, Clement VIII had the book corrected and issued it in 1600.

Errors crept in, so Innocent X had it revised in 1650, Benedict XIII issued a new edition in 1727, and Benedict XIV published an amended and enlarged one in 1741 and 1752. A standard edition of 1886 now rules all others. Its first book covers the bishop's duties, dress, and ministers, and its second the Divine Office and Mass through the year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caesarius-of-:
Caesarius of Prum, born of the noble Milendonk family, was abbot of the rich Benedictine house of Prum near Trier, elected in 1212. Prum then ranked among the richest monasteries in Europe, but many of its monks were noblemen living in comfort, and their example wore down discipline. After five years Caesarius gave up the abbacy to live a stricter life as a humble monk at the Cistercian house of Heisterbach.

At Abbot Kuno's request he wrote in 1222 a commentary on the Register of the Estates of Prum. Drawn up in 893, it has become a key source for thirteenth-century law and civilization. Leibniz and later editors printed the register with his commentary, and recent research also credits him with the history of the abbots of Prum, long assigned to Caesarius of Heisterbach.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-capharnaum:
Capharnaum, also called Kapernaum, was a town of Palestine whose name means village of Nahum, or consolation. The Gospels make it Jesus's home after rejection at Nazareth. There he called Peter, Andrew, James, John, and Matthew as disciples. There he healed a paralytic, Peter's mother-in-law, the centurion's servant, and others. There too he spoke the discourse on the Eucharist.

Its people, urged on by the Pharisees, broke with him, and on leaving he pronounced a curse on the city. Under Constantine a converted Jew named Count Joseph built a church there. Pilgrims visited it into the sixth century. After that the town fades from Palestinian history, surviving now only as a Latin titular see whose exact origin the entry leaves unknown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cariati-pater:
Cariati is a diocese of Calabria in the province of Cosenza, suffragan to Santa Severina, in a healthy site near the sea. Menecrates, present at the Roman synod of 499, is the first bishop on record. Gregory the Great later commended its church to the Bishop of Reggio. A union with the diocese of Cerenza in the eleventh or twelfth century is possible but first appears in record in 1342.

Noteworthy bishops include Polychronius, founder of a monastery at Santa Severina in 1099, and the Cistercian Matteo, who first led the abbey of San Giovanni di Fiore as abbot. The soldier turned nuncio Alessandro Crivello and Fra Filippo Gesualdo, who died in the odor of sanctity, also appear. Pius VII joined Strongoli and Umbriatico to the see in 1818, leaving a diocese of 60,000 people with 28 parishes, 70 churches and chapels, and 61 priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casium:
Casium was a titular see of Lower Egypt near Pelusium, by the sandhills Greek geographers called Kasion Oros, today El-Katieh or El-Kas. A temple of Zeus Kasios, the Aramean god Qasiou, stood there, and Pompey, murdered nearby, was buried at the place. Geographers and church lists name it as a bishopric under Pelusium in Augustamnica Prima, from Georgius Cyprius and Hierocles to a notice of about 840.

Only one bishop is known, Lampetius, who attended Ephesus in 431. Cyril sent him with Hermogenes of Rhinocorura to Rome, where both attended the consecration of Pope Sixtus III. Many letters of Isidore of Pelusium are addressed to Lampetius, whose name survives through that correspondence and the council record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cathedraticum:
Cathedraticum is a yearly sum paid for the bishop's support, given as a mark of honor and a sign of submission to the cathedral church. In the early Church such gifts came by custom rather than law. The earliest law on the subject seems to be a Braga canon of 572. It bound only parish churches and chapters to pay, since the sacraments were then given in parish churches alone.

As other endowed churches and chapels multiplied, Pope Honorius III extended the duty to them as well. The sum was paid at the bishop's annual visitation. The ancient amount was fixed at two solidi, a solidus being one seventy-second of a pound of gold. Later rulings, including decisions of Propaganda, kept the payment a binding law for those concerned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrismarium: A short glossary entry on the chrismarium, a word with two church meanings. In the first sense it is the place in a church set apart for giving Confirmation, where the bishop anoints candidates. In the second sense it is a round jar, usually of silver or pewter, used to hold the holy oils for anointing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ciborium:
An entry on the ciborium, a chalice-like vessel holding the Blessed Sacrament. Some derive the word from Latin cibus, food, for the heavenly bread it holds, while others trace it to Greek kiborion, cup, for its first shape. In early Christian times the term also meant the canopy crowning the altar, but modern liturgical use restricts it to the sacred vessel for reserving the consecrated species.

Today two vessels reserve the Sacrament: the pyx, a small round box for carrying it to the sick, and the ciborium, used for distributing Communion and keeping particles in the tabernacle. Shaped like a chalice with a round bowl, conical cover, and cross, it must be gold or silver, lined with gold within. It is blessed rather than consecrated, and veiled in white silk or cloth of gold while holding the Species. Only sacred ministers may handle it when full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-circesium:
Circesium, a titular see of Osrhoene, was founded under Diocletian and restored by Justinian. Today's identification is Abu Serai, a village on the Euphrates' left bank at the meeting of the Khabur. An older city called Sirhi had stood there before it. Benjamin of Tudela wrongly identified Circesium with Kharkamis, a Hittite capital.

The city was a bishopric in Osrhoene, suffragan to Edessa, and appears only in a list of about 840. Lequien names five bishops, from Jonas at Nicaea, mutilated in an earlier persecution, to Thomas in 553. Fourteen Jacobite bishops are also recorded, from 793 to 1042.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cistercian-ab:
Loccum, in Hanover, a Cistercian abbey of the Minden diocese, was founded in 1163 by Count Wilbrand von Hallermund. From Volkenrode in Thuringia came its first monks, under Abbot Eccardus, placing it in the Morimond line from Citeaux. An old writer calls its site a place of horror and vast solitude haunted by robbers. After want and harsh neighbours, the monks tilled the land and taught the people the fear of God.

The abbey filled its place in Brunswick church life until Lutheranism swept Catholicism from the country. Its chief interest now lies in its buildings, almost perfectly preserved as a Protestant seminary. The cruciform church, built between 1240 and 1277, measures about 218 feet by 110, beside a fine cloister, refectory, chapter-house, sacristy, dormitory, and lay-brothers wing. The head of the house still bears the title of abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-citharizum:
Citharizum, a titular see of Armenia, lay in Asthianene or Balabitene, north of Commagene and Mesopotamia, between Masius and Anti-Taurus. Justinian built a castle there with a garrison under a duke and placed the city in Armenia Quarta, the province he had just formed. In 613 it fell to Ashot, general of the Persian king Chosroes the Second.

Only one bishop is known: Marianus of Kitharizon, named in the records of the Trullan Council of 692. The city appears about 840 in Parthey's first Notitia as part of Armenia Quarta under Melitene's metropolis, it is identified with the modern village of Keterig.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-collectarium:
Augustin Joseph Schulte's entry defines the collectarium, also called collectarius or orationale. It is the book that holds the Collects. In the Roman Missal, the word Statio often stands before the Introit of a Mass. It marks the church where clergy and people once gathered to celebrate the mysteries on a saint's day or feast.

Before walking in procession to that church, they met nearby to receive the pontiff. He recited a prayer called the Collect. The name may come from the assembled people, or from the prayer summing up all favors asked, or from its brief form of the feast's spirit. In time the name spread to prayers before the Epistle, to Secrets and Post-Communions, and to prayers of the Divine Office.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coracesium:
Sophrone Pétridès's entry covers Coracesium, a titular see of Asia Minor. Ptolemy places it not in Cilicia Tracheia but in Roman Pamphylia. It had belonged to Isauria, and from A.D. 74 probably fell within Lycia-Pamphylia. Its port was the Cilician pirates' chief centre. There Antiochus VII killed Diodorus Tryphon, and Pompey destroyed the pirates, levelling their fortress.

Coracesium became suffragan of Side, metropolis of Pamphylia Prima. Lequien mentions only four bishops, the first at Constantinople's Council in 381, the last in 681. The see still appears in the Notitiæ episcopatuum as late as the twelfth or thirteenth century. Today Coracesium is a little town of about 2,000 inhabitants, 500 Greeks, chief centre of a caza in Konia. Its Turkish name is Alaya. Armenians have disappeared, though the town ranked important in the Rupens' time. Curious ruins, walls, and ancient tombs survive, with many romantic stories attached.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cotiaeum:
Cotiaeum, an ancient city of Phrygia Salutaris, claims Aesop as a native son and a long career as a Christian centre. Heresy took root there from the second century, and Socrates records its Novatian bishop. At first a suffragan of Synnada, it rose to an autocephalous archbishopric, then a metropolis with as many as thirteen suffragans.

Ten bishops appear in Lequien's list, the last in the fourteenth century, beginning with Cyrus, sent by Theodosius II after townsfolk slew four bishops. Ruins, a Byzantine castle, and a church survive from antiquity, and Timur sacked the town in 1402. Modern Kutaya, famed for earthenware, counts about 22,000 inhabitants.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-crisium:
A diocesan entry describes Crisium, a Graeco-Slavonic rite diocese in Croatia centred on the little town of Krizevac, north-east of Zagreb. About 1600 many Serbs emigrated from Serbia and Bosnia into Croatia, where they joined earlier settlers called Wallachians. Through Bishop Dimitrovich of Agram, their leader Simeon Vratania gained a monastery and became bishop of the Catholic Serbs in 1611.

His successors stayed loyal to Rome despite schismatic propaganda and conflicts with Agram. In 1671 Bishop Paul Zorcic became vicar-general of Agram for Slavonic-rite Catholics. Only in 1777 did Pius VI re-establish the Uniat diocese as Crisium. Its bishops have resided at Krizevac ever since, serving a flock counted alongside 225,000 schismatics in the territory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-curium:
A short entry describes Curium, a Cypriot titular see suppressed by the papal legate Pelagius in 1222. Legend says Koureus, son of Kinyras, founded Kourion on the south-west coast and settled Argives there in 1595 BC. The city became capital of one of the island's kingdoms.

On the ruined site stands the modern village of Episkopi, near the sea, where Cesnola found the antiquities now in New York's Metropolitan Museum. In the Middle Ages Episkopi passed first to the Ibelin family, then to the Venetian Cornaro, owners of rich sugar plantations. Curium's recorded bishops number only two: Zeno at Ephesus in 431, and Michael in 1051. The tomb of Saint Hermogenes is kept in its church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diaconicum:
An entry on the diaconicum, a word with two linked senses in the Greek Church. As a book it lays out the deacon's functions, and as prayers it names the orations for peace he says before the people. First of all, though, it meant an annex to the basilica where altar supplies were kept and preparations made for the sacrifice.

Prothesis, the small room for receiving the people's offerings, stands distinct from it, and the two commonly flank the apse. A great church's diaconicum majus held several rooms: a reception hall for the bishop, a treasury for vessels and books, and the diaconicum proper. Syrian examples rise two stories on a rectangular plan, and the form recurs in Byzantine churches, African basilicas, and beyond.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didascalia-ap:
The Didascalia Apostolorum claims to be the teaching of the apostles at the Council of Jerusalem. In truth it is a church manual put together in the third century. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry untangles its tangled afterlife, from its first printing in Syriac in 1854. In 1900 scholars found an old Latin version, more than half of which has perished.

The first eight books of the later Apostolic Constitutions simply rework the Didascalia. Scholars can thus rebuild much of the lost Greek original by setting the two texts side by side. The entry leans on the 1906 edition by Funk, and it shows how a manual for early Christian conduct survived in fragments across three tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-docimium:
Docimium was a titular see in Phrygia, a region of Asia Minor. Its coins call its people Macedonians, so it must have been founded by Antigonos Dokimos. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry gives its shifting names, from Dokimeion to Dokimion, and notes its fame for marble quarries. The site is now the village of Istcha Kara Hissar, northeast of Afion Kara Hissar.

Many Christian inscriptions later than Constantine have been found there. Synnada in Phrygia Salutaris held authority over Docimium, whose known bishops number six or seven between 344 and 879, plus one more from an inscription. The entry is a compact study in coins, quarries, and bishop lists fixing a lost city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominus-vobis:
Dominus Vobiscum, Latin for the Lord be with you, is an ancient greeting taken into the liturgy as a prelude to formal prayer. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry traces it to Scripture, to Ruth and Chronicles, and to Christ's promise in Matthew that he is with his people. Church use dates likely from apostolic times, and the Council of Braga named it in 563. It also stands in the Gelasian Sacramentary of the sixth or seventh century.

The phrase bears a deep weight, since the Lord's presence pledges divine protection and earnest of every good gift. The entry follows its place in Mass and office, showing how a few words open the Church's solemn prayers. For readers of the liturgy, it unpacks a greeting heard at every altar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dorylaeum:
Dorylaeum, a titular see in Phrygia Salutaris, Asia Minor, was already an ancient city under Phrygia's kings. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry sets it at Karadja Hissar, six miles southwest of modern Eski Shehir. Near the end of the fourth century before Christ it moved to Shehir Euyuk, where it stayed through the Byzantine age. Known bishops number seven, spanning the fourth through the ninth century.

The most famous, Eusebius, denounced in turn the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches. As late as the twelfth century it still appears among Synnada's suffragans, before fading from record. Seljuk Turks took and destroyed the town about 1070, yet crusaders won a battle there on 1 July 1097, a date the entry preserves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-durham-dunelm:
Durham is an ancient English diocese holding a unique place among bishoprics. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry explains that its border position against Scotland led its bishops to take on political and constitutional roles beside their spiritual office. Their rights were peculiar and wide, and even today the Anglican bishop of Durham ranks above all English prelates save Canterbury, York, and London.

Its line runs back to the Anglo-Saxon see of Lindisfarne, which Saint Aidan founded in 635. Aidan came from Iona at the call of King Oswald of Northumbria to preach to the newly conquered heathen kingdom. He built his monastery on Holy Island, and the entry follows the see from Lindisfarne to Durham through its prince-bishops and their coins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
The ecclesiastical forum is the Church's judicial and coercive power, expressed in the Latin word for a place holding a tribunal of justice. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry argues that this power is plain from the constitution given by the divine founder. As a perfect society, the Church holds within herself all powers needed to guide her members to their appointed end, with a matching right to be obeyed.

That right is called jurisdiction, the source of all church action not drawn from the power of holy orders. It grounds church law, binding both outwardly and inwardly, and from apostolic times rulers have put it into practice. The entry notes that civil encroachment has in our day shrunk the forum in practice, though unwarrantably, to spiritual causes alone.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eusebius-of-d:
Eusebius of Dorylaeum was the layman turned bishop who led the orthodox fight first against Nestorius and then against Eutyches in the fifth century. Trained as an advocate at Constantinople, he publicly challenged a sermon by the chaplain of Nestorius in 423. Later he broke into a sermon by Nestorius himself to protest that the eternal Word had taken a second birth, of a woman, in the flesh. 

As bishop he then turned on his former friend Eutyches, charging him with false teaching before Flavian's synod at Constantinople in 448. Eutyches was condemned, but the council of Ephesus in 449, run by Dioscurus, deposed and banished both Flavian and Eusebius amid cries against him. Eusebius fled to Rome, appealed to Pope Leo, and at Chalcedon in 451 stood as accuser of Dioscurus. He also helped frame the definition of faith that cleared his own name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-flabellum:
The flabellum is a liturgical fan of leather, silk, parchment, or feathers. Deacons waved it at the altar to keep insects from the Sacred Species and the priest. The Apostolic Constitutions of the fourth century already order two deacons to hold such fans. Latin use faded about the fourteenth century; Greek use continues to the present day.

Greek deacons receive the sacred fan at ordination and wave it from Offertory to Communion. Rich examples survive, like the thirteenth-century Kremsmünster fan shaped as a Greek cross. Fans also served as marks of honour: two are borne beside the pope on the sedia gestatoria. In 1902 Leo XIII gave the old Vatican fans to Mrs. Joseph Drexel of Philadelphia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gesta-romanor:
The Gesta Romanorum was a medieval Latin collection of anecdotes, each paired with a moral reflection. It was most likely assembled by a priest late in the thirteenth century or early in the fourteenth. Older guesses that named Berchorius or Helinandus as its author no longer stand. A Catholic Encyclopedia article traces how the book grew, spread, and reached print.

Each tale opened under a heading naming a virtue or a vice. It then told its story and closed with a moral reading, giving preachers ready examples for sermons. Copies multiplied across Western Europe with local additions, and split into three manuscript families. The first printed editions appeared between 1472 and 1475, and an enlarged Vulgate held 181 stories. Poets from Chaucer and Boccaccio to Shakespeare and Schiller later mined the same tales. Many of them survive today inside famous works of European literature.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hadrumetum:
North Africa's Hadrumetum, a Phoenician colony older than Carthage, served Hannibal as a base against Scipio at the end of the Second Punic War. It grew rich under Rome, when Trajan raised it to a colonia. By the third century's end it was capital of the new province of Byzacena. Justinian restored it after the Vandals as Justinianopolis.

Arabs afflicted it again, the Aghlabids rebuilt it in the eleventh century as Susa, Normans held it briefly in the twelfth, and France took it in 1881. Modern Susa counts 25,000 people with a museum, garrison, harbour, and oil wells nearby. The entry closes with nine known bishops between 255 and 551, the last being Primasius, whose works survive in print.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-birn:
Cologne Carthusian Heinrich Birnbaum, born in 1403, entered the order at thirty-two and became a reformer of houses by sheer example. Esteemed for scriptural and theological learning, he was made prior of Mont Saint André at Tournai only three years after entering, in 1438, and held that post eleven years.

Successive priorships at Wesel, Rettel, Trier, Diest, and Liège followed, each house's few abuses yielding to his restoration of St. Bruno's austere discipline, until ill health sent him back to Cologne in 1463. His last decade went to ascetic writings, including a defence of the Immaculate Conception. The entry warns against confusing him with his jurist uncle of the same name, dead in 1439.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hermann-busem:
Hermann Busembaum was a German Jesuit moral theologian, born at Notteln in Westphalia in 1600 and dead at Münster in 1668. He joined the Society of Jesus at nineteen, taught classics, philosophy, and moral and dogmatic theology, and served as rector of the colleges at Hildesheim and Münster. He also became confessor and trusted adviser to Christoph Bernard von Galen, the prince-bishop of Münster.

His lasting fame rests on one short book, the Medulla theologiae moralis, first issued in the mid-1600s. It packs a wide range of moral teaching into a small volume, set out in a clear and orderly way for priests facing hard cases of conscience. Later writers kept adding notes to it, which shows how widely priests used it. Readers meet here a teacher prized for sound judgment, plain method, and practical help.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-homiliarium:
A homiliarium is a collection of homilies, familiar explanations of the Gospels, read with the recitation of the Divine Office. From very early times the Fathers' homilies stood in high esteem for this purpose. Gregory the Great refers to the custom, and Benedict mentions it in his rule, proving it as old as the sixth century.

Homilies of Leo I, terse and suited to liturgy, were prized above others. As new feasts entered the Office, demand for homilies grew, and by the eighth century, the age of liturgical codification, collections began to appear. Many homiliaria survive, and medieval references name many more, including a very old Gallican collection, one by the Roman priest Agimundus, and one compiled in England by Bede.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iconium:
Iconium was a titular see of Lycaonia, which Xenophon calls the easternmost town of Phrygia, while Cicero, Ammianus, and others place it in Lycaonia or Galatia, since provincial boundaries often changed. Anthony gave it to Polemon, dynast of Olbe, who reigned from 39 to 26 BC, and it later joined the Roman province of Galatia, becoming a colony under Claudius.

Paul preached there on his first mission and converted many Jews and pagans, returning soon after to organize the church he had founded, and he elsewhere recalls persecutions endured there. Thecla was one of his converts. Christianized early, Iconium hosted a council in 235 decreeing heretical baptism invalid. Le Quien names thirty-six bishops down to 1721, best known being Amphilochius, friend of Basil and Gregory of Nazianzus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-partibus-i:
An entry on a Latin phrase that once followed the title of a bishop who held a see he could not live in. The phrase means “in the lands of the unbelievers,” and it was added to the names of old Christian sees that had fallen under non-Christian rule. Such bishops were called titular bishops, and the entry sets out how the practice grew.

Early bishops driven out by invaders kept their titles. Other churches gave them shelter. Some even ran empty sees for a time. Later the Church kept the names of lost sees alive by giving them to helper bishops and to bishops in mission lands. The entry traces that shift and dates regular titular appointments to the time of the Twelfth Lateran Council.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-invitatorium:
An invitation to the faithful to join the Divine Office opens this liturgy entry, which takes its name from that call to prayer. Psalm 95, the Venite, has served as the invitation from the earliest times. The life of Porphyrius of Gaza pictures him having it sung so the people could join in, answering Alleluia after each verse. Benedictine practice made it a daily fixture.

In the Benedictine night office the Venite opens the nocturns and is never left out. The antiphons sung with it shift with feasts and weekdays, repeated twice before the psalm and once after the Gloria Patri. Benedict's Rule calls the psalm the Invitatorium, while an older Frankish rule calls it the exhortation response. Readers get a small chant's long history in one place.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-itinerarium:
A prayer for setting out on a journey, printed at the Breviary's end for easy finding, is the itinerarium treated here. Monks and clerics used it before travel, and the custom likely grew from monastic rule. Desert fathers Anthony and Pachomius, and Basil too, legislated in detail how monks should behave abroad, with set duties and restraints for the road.

Benedict's rule shaped Western church custom more than any other. In chapter 67 it ordered that brethren sent on a journey first commend themselves to the abbot's and community's prayers. The community remembered them daily while away. Short absences brought their own customs, the entry notes. Readers get a small prayer set inside a whole discipline of traveling as a monk.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-nepomu:
Johann Nepomuk von Nussbaum was a Munich surgeon who helped bring antiseptic surgery into Germany. Born in 1829, he studied at Munich. He traveled to study under leading surgeons in Paris, Berlin, and Wurzburg. In 1860 he became professor of surgery at Munich, a chair he kept for close to thirty years. His lectures were prized for their practical cast.

After studying under Spencer Wells in England he advanced pelvic surgery, and after learning antisepsis from Lister he spread it through German surgical clinics. His guide to antiseptic wound treatment ran through five editions and was translated into several languages. Among nearly a hundred publications, the best known dealt with ovariotomy, bone transplantation, hernia operations, and cancer treatment. He also served as consultant surgeon-general to Bavarian troops in the war of 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julian-of-ecl:
Julian of Eclanum was the most learned leader of the Pelagian movement. Born about 386, son of Memorius, a bishop in Apulia, he rose through lector and deacon to Bishop of Eclanum about 417. When Pope Zosimus condemned Pelagius in 418, Julian stood among eighteen Italian bishops who refused to sign, and Emperor Honorius exiled them.

Driven from Italy in 421, Julian systematized the teachings of Pelagius and Coelestius and became the party's intellectual chief. For years the struggle was largely a duel between Julian and Augustine, whose works quote Julian's lost books at length. Julian sought reopening of the case under each new pope and met fresh condemnations until his death in Sicily in 454.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-liber-diurnus:
The Liber Diurnus Romanorum Pontificum is a collection of church formularies used in the papal chancery through the eleventh century. It holds models of the chief papers the chancery prepared. They cover a pope's death, election, and consecration, bishops' installation, professions of faith, pallium grants, privileges, dispensations, monastery foundings, property confirmations, chapels, and decrees.

It opens with superscriptions and closings for writing to emperor, empress, Patricius, Exarch, kings, consuls, patriarchs, and clerics. It matters for legal and church history, above all Rome's. Its models come from earlier papal papers, especially Gelasius I (492-496) and Gregory I (590-604). Compiled in the Roman chancery, it began small, grew over time, and has no systematic order. In final form, in two manuscripts at the Vatican and Milan's Ambrosian Library, it dates to the eighth century. Scholars dispute the date: Garnier gives 715, Zaccaria the ninth century, Roziere 685 to 751.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martyrs-of-sc:
Martyrs of Scillium were six Christians condemned to death by the sword at Scillium in 180, by Vigellius Saturninus, proconsul of Africa. Their Acts rank as the most ancient we possess for Roman Africa, and their trial stands out because the accused faced no torture. The proconsul, free of prejudice against Christians, urged them to obey the law and suggested time to think.

The Christians quietly said their minds were made up. Saturninus sentenced the six: having affirmed living as Christians and, offered a remand to Roman life, persisted in contumacy, they must perish by the sword. The dialogue's calm and legal form mark early African martyrdom, showing a magistrate who sought compliance before punishment. Their Acts remain a key source for second-century African Christianity and its clash with Roman authority.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-menologium:
Menologium, also written Menology or Menologe, is in strictness a service book of the Greek Church, though writers have stretched the word to other uses, and this entry chiefly untangles that confusion. From men, a month, the term means month-set: a book ordered by months. Like lectionary, it has borne several quite distinct senses among authorities.

First, Menologium often stands for Menaion. The Menaia, usually twelve volumes, one per month, form an office book matching, very roughly, the breviary's Proprium Sanctorum. They hold the movable parts of saint-day services, above all the canons sung at Orthros, the office matching Lauds. Synaxaries, historical notes on the day's saints, sit between the canon's sixth and seventh odes. Those notes are read much as the day's Martyrology is slipped into Prime in Western offices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-milevum:
Milevum, a titular see of Numidia, appears in Ptolemy's Geography under the name Mileum or Mireon. In the Roman era it was called Colonia Sarnensis Milevitana, after the Sarnus River in Campania, whence its colonists had emigrated, a name often found in the city's inscriptions. With Cirta, Collo, and Rusicade it formed the confederation known as the Four Colonies.

Under Justinian in the sixth century, Milevum gained a strong wall, which survives as a bulwark of the Arab town of Milah. Two councils were held at Milevum, the more famous in 416 against Pelagianism, attended by Augustine and sixty bishops. Its bishops included Optatus, the great opponent of the Donatists, and Severus, Augustine's friend.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-myriophytum:
Myriophytum was a titular see of Thracia Prima, suffragan to Heraclea, whose early history is unknown. It first appears in connection with an earthquake that destroyed it in 1063, and John Cantacuzene visited it about 1350. Under the joint title of Peristasis and Myriophytum it enters an episcopal list near the fifteenth century's end, Peristasis alone dating to 1170.

In the sixteenth century Myriophytum displaced Peristasis in the diocese's name, and in 1908 the Greeks raised it to an autocephalous metropolitan see. Today it is a busy port on the Sea of Marmora counting 5,000 Greeks and 400 Turks. Its schismatic archdiocese holds only ten parishes with about 22,000 souls, Peristasis alone accounting for some 6,000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nahum:
Nahum, seventh in the traditional list of the twelve Minor Prophets, bears a Hebrew name probably meaning full of consolation or comfort, hence consoler or comforter. The name was not rare: Luke's genealogy names a Nahum, the Mishna cites Nahum the Mede, a famous second-century rabbi, and inscriptions show it among Phoenicians.

All we know of the prophet must be gathered from his book, since no other canonical Scripture names him, and extracanonical Jewish writers are hardly less silent. His short prophecy denounces Nineveh, the Assyrian capital, in vivid images of siege and sack, promising Judah's deliverance. The entry weighs its date, its poetry, its place among the prophets, and the city whose fall it celebrates with fierce satisfaction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-neum:
A neum, from Latin neuma or pneuma and Greek pneuma, a nod, is a term in medieval music theory, seemingly unused before the eleventh century. From then it bore two senses: a kind of melody, and a notational sign. Guido of Arezzo takes it in a third sense, comparing music's tones, syllables, neums and phrases to metrics' letters, syllables, feet and verses.

As a melody, a neum is a series of tones sung without words, generally on a text's last vowel. Its older name is jubilus, which Saint Jerome defines as praise beyond words, syllables, letters or speech. Saint Augustine calls it a song of joy without words, fitting above all for the ineffable God. The entry traces neums as notation, from early signs above texts to the staff systems that grew from them, and their role in chant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitia-digni:
The Notitia Dignitatum, or Register of Offices, is the handbook of civil and military posts in the later Roman Empire. Its surviving Latin form dates to the early fifth century, with eastern additions reaching 397 and western notices running into the reign of Valentinian III.

Eastern and western halves each list central officials first, then provincial and diocesan officers, civil beside military, with drawings of their insignia. The chief of the chancery used it to draft appointment notices, and the entry weighs its date, gaps, and value for Roman administration. Its eastern additions reach 397, while western notices run into Valentinian III’s reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-notitiae-epis:
Notitiae Episcopatuum are the official lists that rank metropolitan and suffragan sees in the Eastern churches. Unlike Rome, where rank followed date of consecration, or Africa, where age ruled, the East ranked each bishop by his see: Caesarea first in Constantinople's patriarchate, Ephesus second, and so on.

Each list runs from patriarch through greater metropolitans, autocephalous metropolitans, archbishops, exempt bishops, and suffragans. The entry explains how ranks held unless a later list changed them, and why these lists matter for Eastern church geography. In Constantinople’s patriarchate Caesarea ranked first and Ephesus second among metropolitans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-octavarium-ro:
The Octavarium Romanum, a liturgical book akin to an appendix of the Roman Breviary, supplies lessons for the days within octaves. Sixtus V first ordered such a book for greater variety in lessons, but his plan died with his pontificate from 1585 to 1590.

Under Clement VIII, consultors including Baronius favored the project, and Gavanti carried it out, publishing at Antwerp in 1628 with Urban VIII's brief of approval. Its body gives second and third nocturn lessons for octaves, especially of local patrons and titular feasts. Its title describes lessons for the second and third nocturns within octaves of feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ostensorium:
An ostensorium, from the Latin for to show, is a vessel made to display an object of devotion in plain view. The word and its kin, monstrance, once covered every goldsmith's vessel fitted with glass or crystal to reveal its contents, whether the Sacred Host or a saint's relic. Modern English use narrows both terms to vessels for exposition of the Blessed Sacrament, and the entry keeps to that sense.

Such vessels could only follow the practice of exposing the Sacrament or carrying it in procession, which dates no earlier than the thirteenth century. Lanfranc's rules for Canterbury monks around 1070 already had priests carry a shrine holding the Lord's Body on Palm Sunday, but with no hint that the Host was shown. Later pages trace the shapes of ostensoria, from tower and sunburst forms to modern types, and the rules for their use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pallium:
The pallium is a circular band about two inches wide, worn round neck, breast, and shoulders. Two pendants hang front and back, each two inches wide and twelve long, weighted with lead wrapped in black silk. White wool forms the rest, part of it from two lambs given yearly by the Lateran Canons Regular and blessed on Saint Agnes's feast at Saint John Lateran.

Six small black crosses mark it, one each on breast, back, shoulders, and pendants, with gold pins set with stones on three. The pope and archbishops alone wear it, and archbishops only after leave from the Holy See, and only in their own dioceses on set days. Bishops may receive it as a favour, but it adds no power or rank. Later pages trace its history, symbolism, and rules of use.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paraetonium:
Paraetonium was a titular see of Libya Secunda, or Marmarica, suffragan of Darnis, famed for its port. Some say the city should be called Ammonia. From its harbour Alexander visited the oracle of Amun, and Mark Antony halted there before Actium. Justinian walled it to shield Egypt on the west. It has since vanished, its port partly sand-covered, and its site, long called Baretoun by Arabs, is now Mirsa Berek near Benghazi.

Three bishops are named: Titus at Nicaea in 325, Siras, an Arian, and his successor Gaius at Alexandria in 362.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-parium:
Parium was a titular see, suffragan of Cyzicus in the Hellespont, where a Christian community stood before 180, as the Acts of martyr Onesiphorus prove. Other saints of note are Menignus, martyred under Decius and honoured on 22 November. Theogenes, bishop and martyr, is kept on 3 January. Basil, bishop and martyr of the ninth century, is kept on 12 April.

Le Quien names fourteen bishops, the last living in the mid-fourteenth century, plus an anonymous Latin bishop noted by Innocent III in 1209 and a titular bishop in 1410. Autocephalous as early as 640, Parium stayed so till the late thirteenth century, when Andronicus II raised it to a metropolis as Pegae and Parium. In 1354 both sees were suppressed, the metropolitan taking Sozopolis in Thrace instead. Its ruins lie at Kamares on Cape Tersana-Bournou.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelusium:
Pelusium was an Egyptian frontier city guarding the eastern edge of the Nile Delta. Its name, from a word for mire, matched the marshes around it, and its harbour joined the sea to the Pelusiac branch of the Nile. Pharaohs fortified it, and armies fought over it for a thousand years: Nebuchadnezzar, Cambyses, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes all moved against it before Alexander took it in 333 BC.

Later conquerors kept coming, from Antony and Augustus to the Persian shah Chosroes, the Arab general Amru, and Baldwin I of Jerusalem, who burned it in 1117. When the Nile branch silted up and the sea flooded the land, the city sank into a desert of mud. A ruin-covered hill called Tell Farameh now marks the site. The entry also lists its early bishops and honours St. Isidore, who died there in 450.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philomelium:
Philomelium was a titular see in Pisidia, suffragan to Antioch, on the road from Synnada to Iconium. Ancient writers place it in south-west Phrygia near Lycaonia's border, inside Synnada's judicial district, and its coins show alliance with neighbouring Mandropolis. In the sixth century it belonged to Pisidia, its people pronouncing the name Philomede or Philomene.

Medieval Byzantine historians mention it often in wars against the Seljuk sultans of Iconium. In the twelfth century it ranked among the sultanate's chief cities under the Turkish name Ak-Sheher, White City. Today it is the chief town of its district with 4,000 inhabitants, nearly all Muslims, on the Eski-Shehr to Konieh railway. Seven bishops are known, from Theosebius at Constantinople in 381 to Euthymius in 879, and Smyrna's church wrote to Philomelium of Polycarp's martyrdom in 196.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plenarium:
A plenarium is any book that gathers in one volume material otherwise scattered across several books. The mortuary office as a whole, Vespers, Matins, Lauds, and Mass, was called a plenarium, as was a complete copy of the four Gospels, an evangeliarium plenarium. Examples include the Book of Gospels at Lichfield and the book Athelstan gave to Christ Church, Canterbury.

When priests were scattered singly and private Masses grew common, the complete missal, the missale plenarium, came into use. It held all prayers for Mass that had once been split among sacramentary, lectionary, evangelistary, antiphonary, and gradual. In Germany the name also meant a popular book giving German Epistles and Gospels for Sundays and feasts with short expositions, last printed under that title at Basle in 1522.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polemonium:
Polemonium was a town on the Pontus coast that gave its name to the province of Pontus Polemoniacus. It stood at the mouth of the Sidenus in the region called Sidene, on the site of an older town called Side. It is believed to have taken its new name in honour of Polemon, made king of Pontus by Mark Antony about 36 B.C.

Its harbour gave it some weight, and it is now the village of Pouleman in the Trebizond region, with ruins of an octagonal church and ramparts across the river. Six of its bishops are known, from Aretius at Neocaesarea in 320 to John at Constantinople in 869 and 879, and the see is listed until the thirteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-polystylum:
Polystylum, a titular see in Macedonia Secunda, sat under Philippi. Once Philippi rose to metropolitan rank, Polystylum stood among its subject sees. Leo the Wise's lists near 901, the Nova Tactica near 940, and thirteenth-century records all name it so. Innocent III counted it among Philippi's Latin subject sees in 1212.

Its Greek bishop Peter rose to lead Christopolis in 1363, and Maronia took the see over. Around then Emperor Cantacuzenus rebuilt and walled the town, styling it old Abdera. The entry doubts that styling: Polystylum is present-day Bouloustra, set inland from genuine Abdera's ruins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pretorium:
Pretorium comes from the Latin praetorium, in later Greek to praitorion. At first it meant the general's or praetor's tent in Roman camps. Then it meant the military council judging there, and later the governor's official house, a palace or castle. In the Gospel it marks the house Pilate held at Christ's Passion. Two such castles stood, both built by Herod.

The first rose where the tower of Birah stood, called Baris by Josephus. That tower stood on a rock near the Temple enclosure, cut sheer on the south and parted from Mount Bezetha by a broad ditch on the north. On this rock, now held by Turkish barracks, Herod built a new fort, with two broad courts ringed by porticoes between rock and Temple enclosure.  Herod later built a second palace on Mount Sion's north brow, at the town's west edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-proprium:
The Proprium names the worship texts that change with the day. This encyclopedia entry explains its two blocks: the Proprium de tempore, for the seasons of the church year, and the Proprium Sanctorum, for saints' feasts. Both sit inside the Breviary, the book of prayer, and the Missal, the book of the Mass, supplying introits, prayers, lessons, responses and antiphons fitted to each occasion.

From Advent through Pentecost, the de tempore block maps the church year: Christmas, Septuagesima, Lent, fifty Easter days and the Sundays after Pentecost. Saints' days join the round from Saint Andrew's feast on 30 November. Early Christians knew almost no fixed yearly cycle beyond Easter, Christmas and Sundays, singing psalms and hearing Scripture readings instead. Rome in the fourth century, under Pope Damasus, began fitting prayers to seasons and feasts, and the shared Common of Saints grew from single feasts like those of Peter and Paul.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prum:
Prüm, a former Benedictine abbey in Lorraine now in the Diocese of Trier, was founded on 23 June 720. Its founders were the Frankish widow Bertrada and her son Charibert, with Angloardus as its first head. This encyclopedia entry follows a house that became a Carolingian favourite. Bertrada's granddaughter Bertha married King Pepin. Pepin rebuilt the monastery and showered it with estates in 762. Monks from Meaux under Abbot Assuerus filled its cloister.

The abbey church, dedicated to the Saviour, was finished only under Charlemagne. Pope Leo the Third consecrated it on 26 July 799. Charlemagne and his successors patronized Prüm generously. Several Carolingians took the habit there, among them Lothair the First. He became a monk in 855, and his grave was found again in 1860. Sources from Trier histories to a 1907 chronicle study round out an entry on a monastery woven into Frankish royal history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prusias-ad-hy:
Prusias ad Hypium was a titular see, a bishopric in name, under Claudiopolis in the Roman province of Honoriad. This encyclopedia entry opens with its tangled naming. Prusias the First of Bithynia reigned from 237 to 192 BC. He seized the town of Kieros from the Heracleans, joined it to his kingdom and renamed it for himself. Later copyists confused it with another Prusias, the town of Kios. The entry untangles the two.

Pliny and Ptolemy merely note the place. One sets it below Mount Hypius, the other near the River Hypius. Its known bishops run from George in 325 through Olympus, Dometius, Theophilus, Constantine and Leo. The list ends with Saint Paul, martyred by the iconoclasts in the ninth century. When the see vanished is unknown. French and German travellers and archaeologists, from De Hell to Perrot, supply the entry's sources on this vanished Bithynian town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-psalterium:
The Psalterium, the Book of Psalms as copied and used in worship, is the subject here. As a private prayer book it is treated elsewhere; this entry deals with its liturgical life. In church use it held the bulk of the Divine Office. Companion volumes stood beside it: the Lectionary, the Antiphonary with its Responsoriale, and the Hymnary. For centuries the Western Church sang from two Latin versions, both owed to Saint Jerome.

Jerome revised the older Latin text in 383 at the request of Pope Damasus, following the Septuagint closely, and Rome kept that corrected text for many centuries. In 392 he undertook a fresh version, and the entry follows the fortunes of both texts through medieval manuscripts. Studies of famous copies, from the Bosworth Psalter to the Utrecht Psalter, close a piece for readers curious about the book Christians prayed from day by day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ratio-studior:
Ratio Studiorum, short for Ratio atque Institutio Studiorum Societatis Jesu, names the educational system of the Jesuits. This long encyclopedia entry renders the title as the Method and System of the Society of Jesus's Studies. The Society's Constitutions counted teaching among its chief aims. They list catechism for children and the ignorant, schooling for youth in schools and colleges, and lectures on philosophy and theology in universities. Education stood so high that the Society could rightly be called a teaching order.

Even in Saint Ignatius's lifetime colleges opened at Messina, Palermo, Naples, Gandia and Salamanca, with Ingolstadt foremost among the later foundations. The entry then faces objections to the system. Father Martin, the general of the Society, said in 1892 that the Ratio's marks are not to be sought in its subject matter, nor in the order of its studies, but elsewhere. The entry weighs that claim at length.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regino-of-pru:
Regino of Prüm, Benedictine abbot and writer, died at Trier in 915; his birth date is unknown. Later accounts make him a nobleman's son, born at Altrip's stronghold on the Rhine near Speyer. His life is a blank until his election as abbot of Prüm in 892. His election and his writings show a diligent student who had joined the Benedictine Order, probably at Prüm itself.

Prüm had suffered badly from Norman raids, seized and ravaged in 882 and again in 892. After the second devastation Abbot Farabert resigned, and Regino took his place, labouring to restore the house while rival parties fought over Lorraine. In 899 he was driven from office, and his remaining years connect him with Saint Maximin near Trier. The entry rests on his writings and on later histories of the Trier archdiocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rerum-novarum:
Rerum Novarum, the opening words and title of Leo the Thirteenth's encyclical of 15 May 1891, treats the condition of labour. It follows traditional teaching on property rights and duties and on employer and employee, but applies the old doctrines to modern conditions. Opening with the grievances of the working classes, it refutes Socialist theories, defends private ownership, and seeks the remedy in the joint action of Church, State, employer, and employed.

The Church claims its place because the question bears religious and moral aspects. The State holds the right and duty to intervene for justice and social well-being, while employers and workers should form associations in their own interest. On wages the encyclical admits how hard it is to state justice's full demands, yet growing numbers regard its statement as the most fruitful principle of industrial justice ever uttered.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-responsorium:
The responsory, or respond, is a series of verses and responses, drawn from Holy Scripture and varying with feast or season. Two kinds exist, those of the Proper of the Mass and those of the Divine Office, differing in history and form. The Mass responsory grows from the psalmodic solo, the oldest Christian chant, apparently derived from the Synagogue: one chanter recited the psalm, and the people answered with a refrain.

That refrain might be the psalm's alternate verses, one verse repeated again and again, or a sentence from elsewhere. Psalm Confitemini Domino, with Quoniam in aeternum misericordia ejus answering every verse, is the typical example, though sometimes the refrain was an Alleluia. In the Office the precentor at last began the respond again, singing to the verse, and the choir closed with a repetition. The first responsory of the year, Aspiciens a longe, carried several verses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-gloriose-:
Rex Gloriose Martyrum is the hymn at Lauds in the Common of Martyrs in the Roman Breviary. It holds three strophes of four verses in classical iambic dimeter, rhymed in couplets, with a fourth concluding strophe, a doxology in unrhymed verses varying with the season. Its opening stanza addresses the glorious King of martyrs and crown of confessors, who leads earth-spurners to heaven, and shows the scheme at work.

The hymn's date is uncertain and its author unknown: Mone assigns it to the sixth century, Daniel to the ninth or tenth. The Breviary text revises an older form for classical prosody, changing, for instance, terrena to terrea in the line about spurning earthly things. Manuscript references and readings fill Blume's Analecta Hymnica, and English renderings appear in Donahoe's Early Christian Hymns.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rex-sempitern:
Rex Sempiterne Caelitum is the Roman Breviary hymn for Matins on Sundays and weekdays in Paschal Time, from Low Sunday to Ascension Thursday. Cardinal Thomasius prints its primitive form in eight strophes, and Vezzosi's conjecture identifies it with the hymn Caesarius and Aurelianus of Arles name as Rex aeterne domine in their Rules for Virgins. Pimont agrees, and modern hymnologists confirm the identification without hesitation.

The hymn draws special interest from Bede. In De arte metrica he picks it from many Ambrosian pieces to show the difference between classical iambic metre and the accentual rhythms that imitate it. Bede, usually brief in comment, nevertheless refers to it. English readers meet it in Bagshawe's Breviary Hymns and Missal Sequences and Donahoe's Early Christian Hymns, and Moultrie's translation stands in Bute's Roman Breviary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robber-counci:
The Robber Council of Ephesus, or Latrocinium, was the synod of 449 whose acts survive because they were read aloud at Chalcedon two years later. Convoked by Emperor Theodosius II with the pope's agreement, it met on 8 August 449 under Dioscorus, Patriarch of Alexandria. Western bishops had no time to attend, save Julius of an unknown see, a priest, and the deacon Hilarus, who spoke for Pope Leo.

The question was whether Flavian of Constantinople had rightly deposed the archimandrite Eutyches for refusing two natures in Christ. Flavian and his fellow judges were barred from sitting. Dioscorus refused to have Leo's dogmatic letter read, admitted the monk Barsumas by imperial order, and steered the council to vindicate Eutyches. The rest of the acts survive only in a Syriac version by a Monophysite monk, copied in 535.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-schola-cantor:
A schola cantorum is a place for teaching and practising church chant, or a body of singers joined to render music in church. In the primitive Church clergy sang, but trained singers were brought in to free priests for their proper work. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces the Roman singing school from legend to firm history.

Pope Hilary, who died in 438, is sometimes credited with the first schola, but Gregory the Great, by John the Deacon's account, set the school on a firm footing and endowed it. Sergius II rebuilt its house in 844, having trained there himself, as had Sergius I, Gregory II, Stephen III, and Paul I. The school sang at most papal functions under a prior or cantor, and its chant shaped Western music.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scriptorium:
A scriptorium is commonly a large room in a monastery set aside for the community's scribes or copyists. Where no special room existed, little cells called carrels were built in the cloister, each scribe with his own window and desk. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes the medieval book factory.

Gloucester's cloister, now the cathedral, gives the finest surviving example of carrels. The scriptorium answered to the precentor or his helper the armarius. He supplied desks, ink, parchment, pens, penknives, pumice for smoothing parchment, awls for ruling lines, and reading frames for books to copy. Most supplies were made on site: at Westminster the precentor made ink in the tailor's shop. Rules varied by house, but artificial light was forbidden for copying, and the entry lists the craft's tools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sirmium:
Sirmium, near modern Mitrovitz in Slavonia, claims a church founded by Saint Peter. The Szerém district fell under Kalocsa's archbishop after Hungary's Christianization. In 1228 the archbishop, pleading his diocese's vast extent, asked the Holy See for a new bishopric. In 1229 Gregory IX set up the See of Szerém, covering almost wholly the country on the Sava's right bank.

The see passed under Turkish rule in 1526. From 1537 to 1578 no bishop held it, and after 1624 titular bishops held it. Re-establishment with some territorial changes came in 1709. Clement XIV joined it with Bosnia and Diakovár in 1773, and the entry's sources trace its bishops and fortunes through Farlati's Illyricum Sacrum and Hungarian church histories.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-isidore-of:
Isidore of Pelusium, monk and letter writer of the fifth century, fought unworthy clergy with a voluminous pen. Born at Alexandria late in the fourth century, dying not later than 449 or 450, he left family and possessions for a mountain near Pelusium, whose name joined his own. In the Lychnos monastery he grew remarkable for exact observance and austerity, and a passage in his letters suggests he held the abbot's office. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 warns he is sometimes misnamed Isidore of Damietta.

Facundus and Suidas call him priest, though neither names his church, and he may have been only the monastery's priest. His correspondence shows him battling clerics whose elevation to priesthood and diaconate endangered and scandalized the faithful. Laymen, he complained, avoided sacraments to escape contact with such men. The entry preserves a monk whose letters policed a church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-maris-mar:
Maris, Martha, Audifax, and Abachum were martyred at Rome in 270. This entry tells of a Persian noble family who reached Rome under Claudius II, comforted persecuted Christians, and buried the bodies of the slain. That charity exposed them to the judge Muscianus, who failed to make them give up their faith.

Torture followed, then death: Maris and his sons were beheaded thirteen miles from Rome at Nymphae Catabassi and their bodies burned, while Martha was thrown into a well. A Roman lady named Felicitas rescued the half-burned remains and hid them in a catacomb. Their commemoration is kept on 19 January, leaving the twentieth for Sebastian.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syntagma-cano:
The Syntagma Canonum is a canonical collection made in 1335 by Blastares, a Greek monk about whom nothing certain is known. He aimed to make canon law handier than Photius's Nomocanon and fuller than earlier epitomes by Stephen, Aristenus, and Arsenius. His matter runs in alphabetical order through twenty-four divisions, one per Greek letter, split into 303 titles.

Titles cover civil law as well as church law, some purely one or the other, with church rules quoted from older collections and civil extracts often copied without naming their source. The book soon gained general clerical use and kept authority under Turkish rule. Servian, Bulgarian, and Russian translations followed, and a Servian abridgment entered King Douchan's code of 1349.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-targum:
Targum is the distinctive name for Aramaic translations or paraphrases of the Old Testament. After the exile, Aramaic gradually replaced decaying Hebrew as everyday speech. By the last century before Christ, Hebrew survived mainly in schools and worship. Since most people no longer knew the sacred tongue, Sabbath readings in Hebrew needed an explanatory oral translation. That need created the Targum.

At first only hard passages were rendered, then in time the whole text. The Mishna lays down how the work was done. For Torah readings only one verse at a time went to the translator, for Prophets three, unless a verse stood alone. Some passages were read but not translated. Over-free or allegorical renderings drew warnings. Synagogue Targum was not to be written down, though private and study copies existed early, including one on Job from Gamaliel's day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tavium:
Tavium, or Tavia, was a titular see in Galatia Prima, suffragan of Ancyra. It was chief city of the Galatian tribe of Trocmi, and its place on trade roads made it an important trading post. Coins of Marcus Aurelius and Elagabalus survive. Its temple held a colossal bronze Jupiter, greatly venerated by Galatians. The site is now generally placed at ruins near Nefez Keui, east of the Halys, in a fertile plain.

The ruins, partly reused to build Yuzgad, keep a theatre and possibly a Jupiter temple, with mostly Byzantine inscriptions. The see appears in the episcopal lists to the thirteenth century as Ancyra's first suffragan. Five bishops are named. Dicasius attended Neocaesarea and Nice, Julian the Robber Synod and Chalcedon, Anastasius Constantinople in 553, Gregory the Council in Trullo, and Philaretus Constantinople in 869.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-deum:
The Te Deum is a hymn in rhythmical prose, named from its opening words Te Deum laudamus. Its earliest known title appears in the Rule of St Caesarius for monks, written before 502 when he was Abbot of Lérins. It is also called the Ambrosian Hymn, and the Roman Breviary still styles it the hymn of Ambrose and Augustine at Sunday Matins. Pius X's new Psalterium, printed in 1912, retitled it simply Hymnus Ambrosianus.

Tradition says Ambrose and Augustine composed and sang it alternately on Augustine's baptism night in 387. That tale dates only from the eighth century and is now generally rejected. No early Milan manuscript links the hymn with Milan, and Milan's own eleventh-century breviary gives it no title at all. The entry then traces the hymn's text, use, and many translations, including Luther's German rendering and the English versions based on it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-te-lucis-ante:
Te lucis ante terminum is the hymn at Compline in the Roman Breviary. Ambrose's authorship, defended by Pimont, is rejected by the Benedictine editors and by Biraghi. The hymn appears in an Irish-script hymnary of the eighth or early ninth century. Its classical prosody, with one exception, points to a much earlier origin. In that hymnary it shares Compline with Christe qui lux es et dies.

An earlier arrangement under Caesarius about 502 paired Christe qui lux with Christe precamur adnue at the twelfth hour, alternating through the year. Later the two hymns swapped places by season, with Christe qui lux used in winter and Te lucis in summer and on festivals. Many houses replaced Te lucis with Christe qui lux from Lent to Holy Thursday, as Dominicans still do. Rome assigns Te lucis daily, except from Holy Thursday to the Friday after Easter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-coliseum:
Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre, begun by Vespasian in 72 and dedicated by Titus in 80, is the monument described here. Four stories rise, each in a different order: Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and composite, built of famed travertine. A marshy hollow between Caelian, Oppian, Velian, and Palatine hills, once Nero's Golden House fishpond, gave it ground.

Elliptical in form, 790 feet around, 620 long, 525 wide, and 157 high, it held a wooden arena sanded for gladiators and wild beasts. A low wall and railing shielded crowds, guards patrolled the passage to the podium, and awnings shaded spectators. Later ages quarried it, Christians honoured it, and the entry traces building, games, and ruin with measured detail.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-martyrs-o:
Nineteen Catholics seized at Gorkum in the Dutch revolt are the martyrs of this entry. By 1572 Luther and Calvin had torn much of Europe from the Church, and Calvinism, after its first synod at Embden in 1571, swept the Netherlands. Sea-beggars took Briel in April 1572, then Dortrecht and Gorkum in June, capturing nine Franciscans in the town.

Two lay brothers joined them, with parish priest Leonardus Vechel of Bois-le-Duc, learned at Louvain. Taken to Briel, they were pressed to deny the Eucharist and papal primacy, refused, and were hanged. Canonization, feast, and relics follow, preserving a story of priests and brothers who died for doctrines their captors hated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-themisonium:
Phrygian titular see Themisonium, suffragan of Laodicea, carries a legend of deliverance in this entry. A city of Phrygia near Pisidia's edge, it sometimes counted as Pisidian. During a Gallic invasion, warned by a dream ascribed to Hercules, Apollo, and Hermes, inhabitants fled with wives and children to a grotto thirty stadia away. They set the three gods' statues at its mouth for protection. 

Coins show Lycabas Sozon as the city's god, and the site may match Kara Eyuk Bazar in Smyrna's vilayet. Le Quien names only one bishop, who truly belongs to Temenothyrae. Thampsiopolis, with bishops Zosimus in 451 and John in 869, proves the same see under another name in lists from the tenth to thirteenth centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-of-s:
Monk Theodore of Studium, bold defender of holy images, was the East's last great voice for a free and united Church. Born in 759, he died on the Tryphon peninsula near Akrita on 11 November 826. A high-born, well-schooled man, he counted among his brothers Joseph, Archbishop of Thessalonica. Priest in 781, he took his uncle's place in 794 and pressed for strict keeping of monastic rules.

When Constantine VI put away his wife and wed again, Theodore spoke out, and the emperor sent him to Thessalonica. The emperor's fall brought him home in triumph. In 799 he left Saccudion, threatened by Arabs, and took charge of the Studium house at Constantinople. He gave it a rule that monks across the Byzantine world copied, alive yet on Athos and in Russian houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tradition-and:
Tradition and the Living Magisterium treats how revealed truth reaches the Church apart from Scripture, and who guards it. Tradition, from the Greek paradosis, means both the thing handed down, such as a doctrine, account or custom, and the organ of handing down, the church's preaching. At first only traditions claiming divine origin were in view, then oral tradition distinct from written Scripture.

The question is whether all revealed truth lies in Scripture, or whether Christ gave the apostles divine teachings, by word or inspiration, that they passed on without writing them down. It then treats the living magisterium, the official teaching authority, as the organ that preserves and hands on such truth. Five points follow: its existence and divine founding, its relation to Scripture, how truth lives in the Church's mind, its organization and limits, and the identity of faith through changing formulas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-triduum:
A span of three days chosen for prayer or other devout practice, in private or in public by congregations, parishes, religious communities, seminaries or schools. The three days usually precede a feast, and the feast sets the choice of exercises. Examples are the Holy Week triduum, the Rogation Days, and the litanies before the Ascension.

Church authority also allows tridua for the Holy Trinity, the Holy Eucharist and St. Joseph. The Trinity triduum, instituted by Pius IX on 8 August 1847, may be made at any time of year. The Eucharistic triduum, instituted by Pius X in 1907, falls on the Friday, Saturday and Sunday after Corpus Christi, with sermons and Benediction each day.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-viaticum:
Viaticum is the provision for a journey, in Christian usage the sacrament given to the dying for their passage into eternity. The word comes from Latin viaticus, of or for a road. The entry traces it from Greek farewell suppers and travellers' supplies in Plautus and Pliny to its figurative sense as spiritual strength for life's last journey.

In ancient practice almost any sacrament given at death's door, baptism, confirmation, penance, or anointing, could count as viaticum, but the term settled on the Eucharist received by the dying. Later sections set out the rite in detail, the sickroom's table, crucifix, candles, holy water. Cloth, the altar preparations, and the priest's actions, showing how carefully the Church ordered this final communion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-victor-bishop:
Victor of Tunnunum was a North African bishop and zealous defender of the Three Chapters who died about 569, probably confined in a Constantinople monastery. For refusing Justinian's edict of 544 condemning the Chapters, he was imprisoned at Mandrakion monastery, exiled to the Balearic Islands and then to Egypt.

In 564 summoned with five other African bishops before emperor and patriarch and ordered to submit. All remained obstinate and were confined in separate Constantinople monasteries. Victor's fame rests on his chronicle from creation to 566, of which only the portion from 444 survives. It holds great historical value on the Eutychian heresy, the Three Chapters controversy, the Arians. The Vandal invasion, was first edited by Canisius in 1600, and was newly edited by Mommsen in 1894. A continuation to 590 came from John of Biclar.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zephyrium:
Zephyrium is the Cilicia Prima titular see, suffragan of Tarsus. Nothing is known of its history, though numerous ancient authors mention the city off Cilicia's coast, between Cilicia Tracheia and Pedias. It had many coins, and here was prepared the best molybdenum, white lead, drawn from the neighbouring mines of Coreyra. Today it is Mersina, chief town of a caza in Adana vilayet, with about 14,000 inhabitants, of whom 3,000 are Greeks, 1,000 Armenians, and 650 Catholics, a population growing quite rapidly.

Le Quien names four bishops of Zephyrium: Aerius, present at Constantinople's council in 381, and Zenobius, a Nestorian, at Constantinople's council in 432 to 434. Hypatius, present at Chalcedon in 451, and Peter, at the Council in Trullo in 692, complete the list. Mersina's Latin parish is run by Capuchins, with Sisters of Saint Joseph of the Apparition, schools for boys and girls, and hospitals.
doe-osti-3001271-ab-initio-equation-of-s: Vanadium got its ab initio equation, and this DOE report computes the state from theory. The pages detail the findings. The physicists get their numbers. The element was vanadium. The numbers were physicist. The theory was ab initio. The numbers were theory.
doe-osti-3014292-baseline-cost-model-for: Hydropower costs got baseline-modeled, and this DOE 2025 documentation covers the model. The pages detail the findings. The hydro folks get their data. The year was 2025. The data were hydro. The documentation was model. The model was baseline. The year was DOE's.
doe-osti-3020149-expanding-the-boundarie: Transuranium got boundary-expanded, and this DOE text pushes the chemistry frontier. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their data. The chemistry was transuranium. The data were chemist. The frontier was chemistry. The DOE was text. The chemistry was DOE.
doe-osti-3021386-lithium-divertor-intera: Lithium divertors got helium-trapped, and this DOE final studies lithiated metals. The pages detail the technical findings. The fusion folks get their closeout. The trapping was hydrogen. The closeout was fusion. The metals were lithiated. The report was technical.
doe-osti-3395071-steady-state-radiolysis: Polyhalides got radiolysis-accumulated, and this DOE poster covers steady state products. The pages detail the findings. The chemists get their deck. The format was poster. The deck was chemist. The accumulation were products. The steady were state. The poster were format.
govdocs-archive_org-the-complete-books-o:
Charles Fort collected facts that science would not touch: rains of frogs, objects falling from clear skies, people vanishing and reappearing. The Complete Books of Charles Fort joins his four works in one volume: The Book of the Damned, New Lands, Lo!, and Wild Talents.

Fort called his outcast facts damned data, and he presented them with wit and open contempt for smug experts. He did not prove a theory; he proved a habit of ignoring. That stance made him the father of fortean inquiry, and his books still supply the field's founding cases and its fighting tone.
historia-calamitatum:
Peter Abelard, the medieval thinker, wrote this account of his own misfortunes. The hosted copy is an English translation by Henry Adams Bellows. Abelard tells his life as a letter of comfort to a friend. A long modern essay on his age opens the volume.

Abelard recalls fame in the schools, love, and ruin. One chapter tells how a council forced him to burn his own book. Abbots and brethren then hounded him, he writes, at every turn. The work is frank, proud, and sad at once. It stands among the first true life stories of the Middle Ages.
history-of-the-britons-historia-brittonu:
Nennius, who calls himself a lowly minister and disciple of Saint Elbotus, compiled the History of the Britons in Latin, here translated by J A Giles. His prologue confesses dull intellect and rude speech, and says he gathered the work from ancestors' traditions, writings, and monuments. It is less a history than a heap of British antiquities.

The text gives the Romans, the Saxon advent under Hengist, who demands Kent as his daughter's price through an interpreter, Saint Patrick, and Vortigern. Arthur appears as a war leader winning twelve battles, the earliest Arthur in any history. Brief and credulous as it is, the Historia Brittonum shaped Geoffrey of Monmouth and every later British chronicle.
how-to-write-a-play-letters-from-augier-:
This slim volume gathers letters on playwriting from famed French dramatists. The Dramatic Museum of Columbia University issued it in 1916. William Gillette contributes a piece dated May 1916. Augier, Banville, Dumas, Labiche, Sardou, and Zola are among the letter writers.

Augier answers with a joke about cannon founding. Take a hole, he writes, and pour bronze around it. Whether comedy needs the same core, he leaves open. His one counsel: soak the fifth act in gentle tears, and salt the other four with wit. Labiche gets a warm study as France's richest comic force. Aspiring playwrights got masters' shop talk, brief and bright.
nasa-tm-19650010883-analysis-of-oxygen-i:
Glenn R Zellars compiled the minutes of a NASA round-robin meeting held at Lewis Research Center on June 4, 1964. The subject was measuring oxygen inside potassium metal. Several labs had each analyzed the same potassium samples, then compared results. Groups taking part included Dow Chemical, General Electric, Oak Ridge, and Pratt and Whitney.

Two methods were in use, mercury amalgamation and vacuum distillation. A round-robin test shows whether different labs get the same answer. If they do not, the method needs work. Minutes like these preserve that check in detail, including who took part and what was discussed at the meeting.
nasa-tm-19680001040-thermal-contact-cond:
Harry L. Atkins, of the Space Thermodynamics Branch at Marshall Space Flight Center, reports contract results on how heat crosses a touching joint in vacuum. Two surfaces bolted together pass heat only at scattered contact points. In space, no air helps, so the joint's conductance must be known.

The work plots conductance against applied pressure for four metals. Stainless steel, magnesium, aluminum, and copper samples all appear. Atkins also studies a kink in the aluminum curves when plotted on log-log paper. Squashed cones, hemispheres, and ellipses reproduce the same kink, suggesting scaled-up models of real contact points.
nasa-tm-19680020447-back-flow-from-jet-p:
Norman T. Grier of Lewis Research Center wrote this 1968 paper, TM X-52468, for a July 1968 symposium on rarefied gas dynamics in Cambridge, Massachusetts. His concern is back flow: exhaust gas from a rocket jet that spreads backward in vacuum. Such gas can coat or disturb the very spacecraft that fired the jet.

Grier estimates the back flow density at points level with the nozzle exit plane. His model treats the young plume as a smooth gas flow, then as free flying particles once the gas grows too thin for collisions. He runs the approximate calculation for helium, nitrogen, and argon jets. The result is a practical way to judge a plume's backward reach.
nasa-tm-19690028938-tensile-properties-o:
Adolph C. Spagnuolo and Phillip L. Stone of Lewis Research Center measured the pull strength of pure tantalum in this September 1969 memo. Samples of varied shapes and from varied heats were pulled at high heat. Tests ran in hard vacuum to shield the metal from air.

Peak stress values spread widely among sample shapes at the top test heat. Samples cut from the same heat, by contrast, matched each other well. Tube samples from one heat sat in a narrow strength band. The spread warns engineers to rate tantalum by heat and form, not by book values alone. Tantalum serves in hot aerospace and nuclear gear.
nasa-tm-19700017669-effect-of-adding-lit:
John L. Anderson and Wendell Mayo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in May 1970. It studies a fast-spectrum nuclear critical assembly ringed by molybdenum. The team added four materials, one at a time, and watched the effects.

The added materials were lithium nitride, hafnium, tantalum, and tungsten. For each case the report tracks the fuel loading the assembly needed. It also tracks the resulting neutron energy spectrum, the spread of neutron speeds inside. Such tests guide the design of compact reactors, where each added material changes how the core behaves.
nasa-tm-19710019446-quenching-of-vacanci:
H H Grimes and E R Gotsky of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a September 1971 meeting in Mol, Belgium, on defects in refractory metals. It concerns vacancies, the empty spots left when atoms are missing from a crystal. The team quenched molybdenum, freezing vacancies in place for study. Such defects shape radiation damage, diffusion, and strength in hot metals.

Fast quenching into ultrapure liquid helium had worked well for tungsten. That cold bath keeps the metal clean during the plunge. Earlier teams used the method to measure the energy needed to form a vacancy. Grimes and Gotsky applied the approach to molybdenum, a body centered cubic metal. Their work extended a proven technique to a new material.
pax-vobiscum:
Henry Drummond published Pax Vobiscum in 1890, the second of a series that began with "The Greatest Thing in the World." The title takes Christ's words, "Peace be with you." The book opens on his promise of rest to all who labour and are heavy laden.
